title: AAA — abdominal aortic aneurysm
desc: Abdominal aortic aneurysm — the aorta wider than 3 cm. Rupture risk rises sharply with size.

title: ACoA
desc: Anterior communicating artery — joins the two anterior cerebral arteries; the commonest site of berry aneurysms.

title: Aerated alveolus
desc: An open, ventilated air sac taking part in gas exchange.

title: Afferent arteriole (blood in)
desc: Brings blood into the glomerulus; it constricts or dilates to hold filtration steady.

title: Alveolar duct
desc: Small airway leading into a cluster of alveoli.

title: Alveolar gas
desc: The gas in the air sacs, where oxygen and carbon dioxide exchange with capillary blood.

title: Anterior tibial → dorsalis pedis
desc: Runs down the front of the leg to the top of the foot, where the dorsalis pedis pulse is felt.

title: Aorta
desc: The main artery leaving the left ventricle. Arterial lines and blood pressure measure the pressure in its branches.

title: Aquaporin
desc: Aquaporin-4 water channel. Lets water cross in seconds. Water always moves toward the side with more dissolved particles.

title: Arterial cannula
desc: A 20-gauge cannula in the radial artery. Its trace is only as good as its patency, flush and zeroing.

title: Arterial end
desc: Blood enters the capillary oxygen-rich at arterial pressure.

title: Arteriole — an ABG samples this blood
desc: Arterial blood: an arterial blood gas measures the oxygen, CO₂ and acid–base status delivered to the tissues.

title: Arteriole (from RV)
desc: Pulmonary arteriole bringing deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the capillaries.

title: ASD — atrial septal defect
desc: Atrial septal defect — a hole between the atria. Usually a left-to-right shunt that loads the right heart.

title: Axon
desc: Carries the nerve impulse away from the cell body.

title: Axon hillock
desc: Where the axon leaves the cell body; signals are summed here.

title: Basement membrane
desc: Shared support layer between the alveolar and capillary cells.

title: Basilar
desc: Basilar artery — formed by the two vertebral arteries; it supplies the brainstem and back of the brain.

title: Basilic vein
desc: Superficial vein on the inner side of the arm; a common PICC route.

title: Bile canaliculus
desc: Tiny channel between liver cells carrying bile toward the bile ducts.

title: Bladder
desc: In the pelvis. A full bladder is a good window for seeing pelvic free fluid on ultrasound.

title: Blood around the cells
desc: Capillary blood bringing oxygen and carrying released markers away.

title: Blood escaping
desc: Bleeding continues until the plug and fibrin seal the vessel.

title: Bone marrow
desc: Makes red cells, white cells and platelets; counts fall when it is suppressed or replaced.

title: Bowman’s capsule
desc: The cup around the glomerulus that collects the filtrate.

title: Brachial artery
desc: Main arm artery at the elbow crease; used for manual blood-pressure measurement.

title: Brachial vein
desc: Deep vein paired with the brachial artery.

title: Brain
desc: Uses about a fifth of the body’s oxygen and has no fuel stores, so it depends on steady flow and glucose.

title: Branch to a neighbouring cell
desc: Junction to a neighbouring cell.

title: Ca²⁺ channel
desc: L-type Ca²⁺ channel. Opens during each beat; the Ca²⁺ that enters triggers contraction.

title: Capillary: RBCs load O₂ in the first third of their transit
desc: Red cells normally finish loading oxygen early in the capillary, leaving reserve time for exercise or thickened membranes.

title: Cardiac muscle cells
desc: Heart muscle cells, joined end to end so the beat spreads as one.

title: Celiac trunk / SMA
desc: The first two gut branches of the abdominal aorta: celiac (stomach, liver, spleen) and superior mesenteric (small bowel, right colon).

title: Cell membrane
desc: A lipid bilayer that keeps ions apart; channels and pumps in it control what crosses.

title: Central line (right IJ)
desc: Central venous catheter in the right internal jugular vein, transduced to give the CVP trace on the monitor.

title: Central line enters here
desc: Puncture site for the right internal jugular approach: the straightest route to the SVC and right atrium.

title: Centrioles
desc: Organises the spindle that separates chromosomes when the cell divides.

title: Cephalic vein
desc: Superficial vein on the outer (thumb) side of the arm.

title: Cholesterol
desc: Sits among the lipids and stiffens the membrane.

title: Clot at the catheter tip
desc: Clot at the cannula tip damps the trace: systolic falls, diastolic rises, and the dicrotic notch disappears. Aspirate and flush.

title: Collapsed
desc: Alveolus with no air (atelectasis): blood flowing past it is not oxygenated — shunt.

title: Colon
desc: Large bowel framing the abdomen; it can perforate or lose its blood supply.

title: Common carotid artery
desc: Main artery of the neck, medial and deep to the internal jugular vein; pulsatile and not compressible.

title: Common iliac artery
desc: One of the two branches the aorta splits into at the level of the umbilicus.

title: Core and penumbra
desc: Core: tissue already dead. Penumbra: tissue that is failing but salvageable if blood flow returns soon.

title: CVC tip at the cavo-atrial junction
desc: Central line tip at the cavo-atrial junction (lower SVC). Here it reads true central venous pressure and is safe for vasopressors.

title: CVC tip in the right ventricle
desc: The catheter has gone too far — into the right ventricle. Expect ectopics and a ventricular-shaped pressure trace; pull it back to the cavo-atrial junction.

title: Cytosol
desc: The fluid inside the cell: high potassium, low sodium and calcium.

title: Deep femoral (profunda) artery
desc: Deep branch of the femoral artery supplying the thigh.

title: Dendrite
desc: Receives signals from other nerve cells.

title: Dendrites
desc: Branches that receive signals from other nerve cells.

title: Dendritic spines (synapses land here)
desc: Small knobs on dendrites where synapses land.

title: Dependent lung
desc: The lowest lung regions (the back, when supine), where oedema and collapse concentrate under gravity.

title: Diaphragm
desc: Dome-shaped muscle separating chest from abdomen; fluid is looked for just above and below it on ultrasound.

title: Efferent arteriole (blood out)
desc: Carries blood out of the glomerulus; its tone helps set filtration pressure.

title: Endothelium (vessel wall)
desc: The single cell layer lining blood vessels; it controls leak, tone and clotting.

title: External carotid → superficial temporal
desc: Supplies the face and scalp; its terminal branch, the superficial temporal, is felt in front of the ear.

title: External iliac artery
desc: Continues from the common iliac into the leg as the femoral artery.

title: External jugular vein
desc: Superficial neck vein crossing the sternocleidomastoid; its filling is a rough bedside sign of venous pressure.

title: Extracellular fluid
desc: The fluid outside cells (plasma and interstitial fluid): high sodium and chloride, low potassium.

title: Facial artery
desc: Branch of the external carotid crossing the jaw in front of the masseter.

title: Facial vein
desc: Drains the face into the internal jugular vein.

title: Fatty-acid tails · oily core
desc: The oily middle of the bilayer that ions cannot cross without a channel or pump.

title: Femoral → popliteal vein
desc: The deep vein of the thigh, continuing behind the knee as the popliteal vein; a common site for DVT.

title: Femoral artery
desc: Main leg artery in the groin; an alternative arterial-line site and a pulse to feel in shock.

title: Femoral vein
desc: Large vein in the groin, medial to the femoral artery; a quick central-access site in emergencies.

title: Fibrin mesh
desc: Fibrin strands from the clotting cascade bind the plug into a firm clot.

title: Flooded
desc: Alveolus filled with fluid (oedema or pus): no gas exchange, a shunt that extra oxygen barely helps.

title: Free air
desc: Gas outside the bowel, under the diaphragm — a sign of perforation needing surgery.

title: Free ribosomes
desc: Free ribosomes make proteins that stay inside the cell.

title: Glomerulus (capillary loops)
desc: A knot of capillaries where plasma is filtered into the tubule.

title: Glycocalyx
desc: A sugar coat on the outer surface; in vessels it helps keep fluid inside the circulation.

title: Glycogen granules
desc: Stored glucose, released when the cell needs fuel quickly.

title: Golgi apparatus
desc: Sorts, finishes and ships proteins made in the ER.

title: Great saphenous vein
desc: Long superficial vein on the inner leg, from the ankle to the groin.

title: Heart
desc: Injured heart muscle releases troponin; a stretched heart releases natriuretic peptides.

title: Hepatocytes (liver cells)
desc: Liver cells that make proteins and clotting factors, process drugs and store glycogen.

title: Iliac veins
desc: Drain the legs and pelvis into the inferior vena cava.

title: Inferior vena cava
desc: Drains the legs and abdomen into the right atrium. On ultrasound its size and change with breathing reflect right-atrial pressure.

title: Initial segment (spike starts here)
desc: Axon initial segment — packed with sodium channels; the action potential starts here.

title: Injured cells leak AST/ALT
desc: Damaged liver cells release their enzymes (AST, ALT) into the blood.

title: Inner leaflet (PE, PS⁻)
desc: The inner lipid layer, rich in negatively charged phosphatidylserine.

title: Intercalated disc → next heart cell
desc: Intercalated disc — junctions that link heart cells mechanically and electrically.

title: Internal carotid artery
desc: Branch of the common carotid that supplies most of the brain hemisphere.

title: Internal iliac artery
desc: Supplies the pelvic organs; a source of bleeding in pelvic fractures.

title: Internal jugular vein
desc: Drains the brain and face; lies beside the carotid artery and collapses with probe pressure.

title: Interstitium
desc: Space between alveolus and capillary. It swells with fluid in oedema and thickens in fibrosis, slowing gas diffusion.

title: IVC
desc: Inferior vena cava — carries blood from the lower body to the right atrium, just right of the aorta.

title: K⁺ channel
desc: K⁺ leak channel (Kir2.1). Open at rest. K⁺ leaks out down its gradient and takes positive charge with it — this sets the resting potential.

title: Kidney
desc: Filters about 180 L of plasma a day; creatinine and urea rise when filtration falls.

title: L kidney
desc: Left kidney — retroperitoneal, behind the spleen and bowel.

title: LA
desc: Left atrium — receives oxygenated blood from the four pulmonary veins and fills the left ventricle through the mitral valve.

title: Left ventricle
desc: Thick-walled pump that generates systemic pressure and pushes blood into the aorta.

title: Lining fluid
desc: Thin liquid layer on the alveolar surface. It thickens and floods in pulmonary oedema.

title: Lipofuscin (aging pigment)
desc: Brownish wear-and-tear pigment that builds up in long-lived cells.

title: Liver
desc: Largest solid organ, under the right ribs. Makes clotting factors and albumin, clears lactate and drugs; a common source of bleeding in blunt trauma.

title: Low V/Q
desc: Alveolus that gets less air than blood. Oxygen falls but improves with supplemental oxygen.

title: LV
desc: Left ventricle — the high-pressure pump for the whole body; its wall is about three times thicker than the right ventricle’s.

title: Lymphocyte
desc: White cell of the adaptive immune system (T and B cells).

title: Lysosome
desc: Lysosome — breaks down worn-out parts and engulfed material.

title: Median cubital vein
desc: Links cephalic and basilic veins at the elbow — the usual venepuncture site.

title: Microtubules (cytoskeleton)
desc: Microtubules — internal scaffolding and tracks for moving cargo.

title: Mitochondria (~30 % of the cell)
desc: Mitochondria make ATP using oxygen. Heart cells are packed with them because they never rest.

title: Mitochondria (make ATP)
desc: Make ATP from oxygen and fuel; without oxygen the cell falls back on inefficient glycolysis and makes lactate.

title: Morison’s pouch
desc: The space between liver and right kidney — the lowest upper-abdominal space when supine, so free fluid collects here first.

title: Mucus plug
desc: Mucus blocking a bronchus: the lung beyond it collapses and shunts blood, so oxygen falls.

title: Myelin sheath (glial cell)
desc: Insulating wrap from glial cells that speeds conduction.

title: Myofibrils (sarcomeres)
desc: Bundles of sarcomeres — the contractile machinery of a muscle cell.

title: Na⁺ channel
desc: Voltage-gated Na⁺ channel (Nav1.5). Opens at threshold to fire the cell. If the resting potential drifts up, its inactivation gate shuts and stays shut.

title: Na⁺/K⁺ pump
desc: Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase (sodium–potassium pump). Uses one ATP to push 3 Na⁺ out and bring 2 K⁺ in. Sped up by insulin and β₂-agonists; needs Mg²⁺.

title: Na⁺/K⁺ pumps (in the membrane)
desc: Use ATP to keep sodium out and potassium in, maintaining the resting potential and cell volume.

title: Neurofilaments & microtubules
desc: Neurofilaments and microtubules — the axon’s skeleton and transport tracks.

title: Neuron cell body
desc: The part of a nerve cell containing the nucleus.

title: Neutrophil (white cell)
desc: The commonest white cell; first to arrive at infection and injury.

title: Nissl bodies (rough ER)
desc: Nissl bodies — stacks of rough ER that make a neuron’s proteins.

title: Node of Ranvier
desc: Node of Ranvier — a gap in the myelin where the impulse is regenerated.

title: Nuclear envelope & pores
desc: Double membrane around the nucleus; its pores let RNA and proteins in and out.

title: Nucleolus
desc: Inside the nucleus; builds ribosomes.

title: Nucleus
desc: Holds the cell’s DNA and controls which proteins are made.

title: O₂ leaving for the tissue
desc: Oxygen unloads from haemoglobin where tissue oxygen levels are low.

title: Osmolyte channel
desc: Osmolyte channel (VRAC). Over ~48 h brain cells shed (or rebuild) organic osmolytes so their volume returns to normal.

title: Outside the cell
desc: Extracellular fluid — high in sodium and chloride, low in potassium.

title: Pancreas
desc: Lies behind the stomach across the spine. Inflamed in pancreatitis, it can leak fluid into the retroperitoneum.

title: PDA — patent ductus arteriosus
desc: Patent ductus arteriosus — the fetal channel between the pulmonary artery and aorta that normally closes after birth.

title: Pelvic fluid
desc: Free fluid behind the bladder (or uterus) — the lowest part of the peritoneal cavity.

title: Peroxisome
desc: Peroxisome — breaks down fatty acids and toxic peroxides.

title: PFO — patent foramen ovale
desc: Patent foramen ovale — a flap-valve between the atria left over from fetal life. It opens right-to-left when right-atrial pressure exceeds left (e.g. high PEEP, PE).

title: Phlebostatic axis
desc: Fourth intercostal space, mid-axillary line — the level of the right atrium. Transducers are levelled here.

title: Phospholipid heads
desc: Water-loving heads facing the fluid on each side of the membrane.

title: Plasma
desc: The liquid part of blood, carrying dissolved gases, proteins, electrolytes and clotting factors.

title: Platelet
desc: Cell fragment that sticks to exposed collagen and starts a clot.

title: Platelet plug
desc: Platelets stacked at the injury — the first, temporary seal.

title: Pleural air
desc: Air between the lung and chest wall (pneumothorax). Under tension it compresses the lung and kinks venous return.

title: Popliteal artery
desc: Artery behind the knee, continuing from the femoral.

title: Portal vein
desc: Carries blood from the gut and spleen to the liver; not a systemic vein.

title: Posterior tibial artery
desc: Runs behind the inner ankle bone, where its pulse is felt.

title: Pressure bag
desc: Pressurised flush bag (about 300 mmHg) that keeps the line open with a slow continuous flush. Below about 250 mmHg blood can back up the line.

title: Pulmonary arteriole: mixed venous blood
desc: Blood returning from the whole body, low in oxygen and high in CO₂, arriving to be re-oxygenated.

title: Pulmonary artery
desc: Carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs. A pulmonary-artery catheter sits here.

title: Pulmonary veins
desc: Four veins that return oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium.

title: Pulmonary venule: arterialised blood
desc: Blood leaving the lung after gas exchange, now carrying oxygen at arterial levels.

title: R kidney
desc: Right kidney — retroperitoneal, so bleeding from it does not show on FAST.

title: RA
desc: Right atrium — receives venous blood from the body and passes it through the tricuspid valve to the right ventricle.

title: Radial arterial line
desc: Cannula in the radial artery, transduced to give beat-to-beat blood pressure and easy blood sampling.

title: Radial artery
desc: Wrist artery on the thumb side; the usual arterial-line and ABG site because the hand also has the ulnar supply.

title: Recruited
desc: An alveolus reopened by pressure (PEEP or a recruitment manoeuvre).

title: Red blood cell
desc: Carries oxygen bound to haemoglobin and gives some of it up in the tissues.

title: Red cell
desc: Red blood cell — carries oxygen bound to haemoglobin.

title: Renal artery & vein
desc: Supply and drainage of the kidney; the kidneys receive about a fifth of the cardiac output.

title: Renal vein: reclaimed / new HCO₃⁻
desc: The kidney returns filtered bicarbonate and makes new bicarbonate, correcting metabolic acidosis over hours to days.

title: Retroperitoneal haematoma
desc: Blood behind the peritoneum (e.g. from the aorta, kidney or pelvis). FAST cannot see it; CT can.

title: Right atrium
desc: Collects venous blood from the body (via the superior and inferior venae cavae) and the heart itself. Its pressure is the central venous pressure.

title: Right internal jugular vein
desc: Large vein lateral to the carotid in the neck; the usual site for an ultrasound-guided central line.

title: Right ventricle
desc: Thin-walled pump that sends blood into the low-pressure lungs. It copes poorly with a sudden rise in pulmonary pressure (PE, high PEEP, ARDS).

title: Rough ER + ribosomes
desc: Rough endoplasmic reticulum — studded with ribosomes that make proteins for membranes and export.

title: RV
desc: Right ventricle — pumps blood into the pulmonary artery and lungs; thin-walled and sensitive to afterload.

title: Sarcoplasmic reticulum
desc: Sarcoplasmic reticulum — stores calcium and releases it to trigger each contraction.

title: Secretions narrow the tube
desc: Secretions inside the endotracheal tube raise airway resistance: peak pressure rises while plateau pressure stays the same.

title: Sinusoid (blood)
desc: Leaky liver capillary where blood bathes the hepatocytes.

title: Small bowel
desc: About 6 m of bowel in the middle of the abdomen; obstruction or loss of blood supply (mesenteric ischaemia) makes it dilate and leak.

title: Small saphenous vein
desc: Superficial vein on the back of the calf, joining the popliteal vein.

title: Smooth ER
desc: Smooth endoplasmic reticulum — makes lipids and stores calcium.

title: Spleen
desc: Under the left ribs; blood-filled and the organ most often injured in blunt abdominal trauma.

title: Splenorenal
desc: The space between spleen and left kidney, the left-upper-quadrant FAST window.

title: Stomach
desc: Upper-left abdomen. Air in it is normal; air outside it (free air) means a perforation.

title: Stopcock open to air
desc: The transducer is open to atmosphere, so the monitor reads zero. Turn the stopcock back to the patient.

title: Striations (sarcomeres)
desc: Repeating contractile units that give heart and skeletal muscle their striped look.

title: Subclavian → axillary artery
desc: Supplies the arm; it lies just behind the subclavian vein.

title: Subclavian → axillary vein
desc: Runs under the clavicle into the arm; an alternative central-line site with lower infection risk but a pneumothorax risk.

title: Superior vena cava
desc: Drains the head, neck and arms into the right atrium. A central line’s tip belongs in its lower part, near the right atrium.

title: Surfactant
desc: A film that lowers surface tension so small alveoli stay open. Deficient in premature lungs and damaged in ARDS.

title: SVC
desc: Superior vena cava — drains the upper body into the right atrium; the target vessel for a central line tip.

title: T-tubules (at each Z line)
desc: T-tubules carry the electrical signal deep into the cell so all sarcomeres contract together.

title: Tear — collagen exposed
desc: A break in the vessel wall exposes collagen, which triggers platelets and clotting.

title: Thick RV wall
desc: Right-ventricular hypertrophy — the RV wall thickens when it has to pump at high pressure (outflow obstruction, pulmonary hypertension, a large VSD).

title: Tibial veins
desc: Deep veins of the calf, paired with the tibial arteries.

title: Tissue (muscle) — uses the O₂
desc: Working tissue takes up oxygen; how much depends on its demand and the flow it receives.

title: Transducer level
desc: Where the transducer sits relative to the phlebostatic axis. Every 10 cm below the axis adds about 7.4 mmHg to the reading; above, it subtracts.

title: Transport vesicles
desc: Small membrane bubbles carrying proteins between compartments and to the surface.

title: Tricuspid valve
desc: Three-leaflet valve between the right atrium and right ventricle. If it leaks, the CVP waveform shows tall v waves.

title: Tubule — filtrate → urine
desc: Reabsorbs most of the filtrate — water, sodium, bicarbonate, glucose — and adjusts what stays as urine.

title: Type I cell
desc: Very flat cell forming most of the alveolar wall — the thin barrier gas crosses.

title: Ulnar artery
desc: Wrist artery on the little-finger side; the back-up supply to the hand when the radial artery is cannulated.

title: Urine: H⁺ excreted as NH₄⁺ / H₂PO₄⁻
desc: Acid leaves the body in urine bound to ammonia and phosphate buffers.

title: Venous end
desc: Blood leaves the capillary with less oxygen and more CO₂.

title: Ventilation: fresh gas in, CO₂ out
desc: Breathing replaces alveolar gas: it brings oxygen in and washes carbon dioxide out. CO₂ removal depends on minute ventilation.

title: Venule — a VBG samples this blood
desc: Venous blood: a venous gas tracks pH and CO₂ reasonably well but says little about oxygenation.

title: Venule (to LA)
desc: Pulmonary venule carrying oxygenated blood back toward the left atrium.

title: VSD — ventricular septal defect
desc: Ventricular septal defect — a hole in the septum between the ventricles. Flow normally runs left to right; it reverses if right-sided pressures exceed left.
